about: Section 10 of notebooks/learning/cost_speed_quality.ipynb, run live: GPT-5.4 mini on Microsoft Foundry, 5 inline calls, then 20 questions as one batch, then one GPT-5.4 judge batch (fitted to live answers). Written by the MLflow runs 'answer gpt-5.4-mini · foundry inline · tutor Ask · dev-5' and 'answer gpt-5.4-mini · foundry batch · tutor Ask · dev-20'. Endpoint and resource names are left out on purpose.

sort_changes/check:0:1.text:
“`The eval set, since it may be too small to trust`” gets one thing right: a small eval set can make patterns noisy, so you should be cautious.

But it misses the main clue in this lesson. If most regressions are in the “same articles, different answer” bucket, the articles were the same and the change happened after retrieval. That points away from the eval set itself and toward `generation` — the step where the model writes the answer. The issue is more likely the prompt, the model, or the scorer.

So `generation` is better because the traces already show retrieval stayed the same, and the answer still changed.

claim_gate/check:2:2.text:
“Release, since most are supported” gets one thing right: it notices that some claims are fine. But it misses the safety rule. A safe gate does not vote by majority. One `contradicted` claim means the answer says the opposite of the source, so the whole answer is not safe to show.

`Abstain, since one claim is contradicted` is better because it follows the gate’s rule: if any claim is `contradicted`, do not release anything, even if the other claims are `supported`.

field_status/check:2:1.text:
`DROPPED: nothing uses it yet` gets one part right. You have not seen the runbook or module use the field yet. So it is fair to say, “I do not see it used so far.”

But it misses the key point. `DROPPED` means you already know the field was accepted, then not passed on, and then ignored on the way to the provider. Here, you have not traced that far. The field may still be used later. So “dropped” is too certain.

`UNKNOWN: not traced all the way yet` is better because it says the truth: the check accepted it, but you do not yet know whether the runbook, module, or provider will use it.

peak_capacity/check:0:2.text:
That guess gets one thing right: it points to a limit problem. But it gets the reason wrong. Tokens do not cost more in the morning. The limit is not usually smaller then. What changes is the load. More users arrive at once, so the minute gets busier and can hit the `TPM` limit, which means tokens per minute.

The better answer is: “It was sized from the daily average, not the busiest minute.” That matters because a calm average can hide a morning burst.

So the lesson is about traffic shape, not token price. If you want, I can help you turn that into a one-sentence exam answer.

wilson_interval/check:0:0.text:
“The leak rate is 0%” gets one thing right: in the 30 test prompts, none slipped through. But it misses the main point. `0` out of `30` does not prove the true leak rate is exactly `0%`. It just means the sample saw no leaks, and with a small sample there is still uncertainty.

So, “The leak rate is probably low, but could be as high as about 11%” is better because it is honest about that uncertainty. It says what the data suggests, without pretending the true rate must be zero.

What would you say if you had only `3` safe tests instead of `30`?

claim_gate/check:2:2.text:
`Release, since most are supported` gets one part right: the other claims are fine. But it misses the safety rule. A single `contradicted` claim means one statement says the opposite of its source passage, so the answer is not safe to send as-is.

That is why `Abstain, since one claim is contradicted` is better. A safe gate does not pick the “best average” answer. It stops when any claim is contradicted, because that means the response contains a wrong statement.

replay_tools/check:0:0.text:
“Nothing: B scored higher, so B wins” gets one thing right. It notices that `B` had the better score.

But it misses the real problem. The two runs did not see the same world. The tools read live order data, and that data changed between Monday and Tuesday. So the scores are not a fair comparison of the agent designs.

“The live orders changed between the runs” is better because it names the cause of the unfair test. It tells you the difference came from the data, not from the agent.

field_status/check:2:1.text:
`DROPPED: nothing uses it yet` gets one idea right. You have not seen the field used by the runbook or the module yet.

But it misses the key point. `DROPPED` means the field was seen and then not passed on. Here, you have not traced that far. The check only said the field is allowed. After that, you still do not know whether the runbook will keep it, change it, or ignore it. So `DROPPED` jumps too far.

`UNKNOWN: not traced all the way yet` is better because it says the field may still matter, but you have not followed it to the provider yet.

fluke_risk/check:2:0.text:
`Run all 50 on the holdout set` gets one thing right: it uses the holdout set, which is the set kept aside for the final check. But it misses the main risk. If you try 50 ideas on that same set, you are no longer doing a clean final check. You are letting many tries “peek” at the answer key, so one idea may look good by luck.

That is the multiple comparisons problem. More tries means a higher chance that at least one wins by chance.

`Test fewer, with a stricter bar` is better because it limits how many ideas you compare, and it makes it harder for a lucky result to count as a win. Then you confirm the best one only once on the holdout set.

peak_capacity/check:0:2.text:
That answer gets one thing right: it notices there is a limit, and that a limit can cause `429` errors. But “tokens cost more in the morning” is not the reason. Tokens do not get more expensive by time of day. The problem is that more users arrive in that morning burst, so the model gets more requests per minute than the average suggests.

“It was sized from the daily average, not the busiest minute” is better because it matches the real mistake in the lesson: the system looked calm on average, but it was overloaded during the peak minute, so it hit the `tokens-per-minute` limit.

What makes the busiest minute matter is the short spike, not token price.

Do you want to try explaining why the `gateway` can also return `429`, even if the model quota is high?

dedupe_chunks/check:0:2.text:
“Use a bigger model” gets one thing right: a stronger model can sometimes understand messy text better. But it misses the real problem here. The issue is not that the model is too weak. The problem is that the index is full of repeated chunks, so the same disclaimer keeps winning the search.

“Remove duplicate chunks before indexing” is better because it fixes the source of the waste. You store one copy of each cleaned text, so you pay for fewer embeddings and give useful chunks a better chance to show up.

In this lesson, `dedupe_chunks` should keep the first chunk for each cleaned key and skip later repeats.

A `key` is just a normalised version of the text. That means lowercase, and extra spaces or line breaks squeezed into single spaces.

Want a quick memory trick for this check question?

ablation_report/learn:stops.text:
Yes. This lesson can stop being enough in a few common cases.

If the app changes over time, the old eval can lie. For example, a `reranker` may look useful today, then become less useful after the search data changes. Re-run ablations often, and use fresh test questions.

If you have very little data, a 1-point drop may just be noise. Then one removed part can look important by chance. Use more questions, or repeat the eval and look for the same drop again.

If the system is much bigger, parts can help only together. A `rewrite` step may seem useless alone, but help a lot when paired with `memory`. In that case, test combinations too, not just one part at a time.

Which of your parts feels most uncertain right now?

fluke_risk/learn:term.text:
`Design` and `Bonferroni` are different guards.

`Design` is the planning step. It says: do not test too many variants. Test only a few. That lowers the chance of being fooled by luck.

`Bonferroni` is a stricter rule inside `Design`. If you do make several comparisons, it splits the usual 5% false positive limit across them. So with 20 comparisons, the lesson says to use about `0.25%` for each one.

They work together. `Design` reduces the number of chances for luck to sneak in. `Bonferroni` makes each chance harder to win.

Everyday example: if you taste 20 soups, one may seem best just by accident. `Design` says “taste fewer soups.” `Bonferroni` says “if you taste many, be much more strict about calling one the winner.”

In the lesson’s example, 20 variants give about a `64%` chance that at least one looks like a winner by luck. `Bonferroni` lowers the per-variant cutoff, and the holdout set confirms the winner once.

run_tokens/check:0:1.text:
`Output tokens cost less than input tokens, per token` is not the best answer here. It gets one thing right: model output is often priced lower than input. But that is not the main mistake in the teammate’s estimate.

The main miss is the **running total**. An agent does not just make 6 separate first calls. It sends back the whole `context` each time, including earlier instructions, answers, and tool results. So later steps are bigger.

So `Each step resends everything that earlier steps added` is better, because it explains why the cost grows across the whole run, not just why output may be cheaper.

What does the lesson say the teammate forgot to include in their estimate: pricing, or the growing `context`?

smoke_set/check:2:2.text:
“Ship it and see what users say” gets one thing right: real users do give real feedback. But it misses the main point here. A score of `12 to 28` on the smoke set means the new idea is clearly worse. The smoke set is a fast filter for bad ideas. It is not the place to hope the result changes in production. Shipping now would waste time, money, and user trust.

“Drop it and try the next idea” is better because it stops a weak idea early and keeps you moving.

dollars_per_success/learn:term.text:
`Cost per success` means: how many dollars you spend for each task that ends up passing.

In plain words, it asks, “If I want one good result, what does that cost me?”

This lesson uses it as:
- total spending, including failed runs
- divided by the number of passed runs

So in the example:
- `one agent` costs `$0.50` and passes `6` tasks
- `team` costs `$5.90` and passes `8` tasks

Their cost per success is:
- `one agent`: about `$0.50 / 6 = $0.08` per pass
- `team`: about `$5.90 / 8 = $0.74` per pass

So the team passes more tasks, but each passed task costs much more. That is why the lesson also asks for the cost of each extra pass.

guard_destroys/check:1:1.text:
“Only if the reviewer turns it on” gets one part right: a reviewer can choose to look at a plan policy or skip it.

But it misses the main point of the lesson. A `plan policy` is not a manual checklist. It runs by itself on every Spacelift run. That means it still checks the Friday evening `plan` even if the reviewer is tired or misses something.

So the better idea is: `Yes, it runs on every run by itself.`  
That matters because it protects the things you cannot easily rebuild, like Azure Databricks workspaces, storage accounts, and metastores, even when people are busy.

callable_tools/check:0:2.text:
“SQL functions cannot be called once an agent is deployed” is too broad. It gets at the real symptom: the notebook test can work while the deployed agent fails. But the cause is not that the function is SQL. A SQL function can be called by an agent if permissions are set right.

What it misses is the permission split between the person testing and the deployed agent. The deployed agent usually runs as a `service principal`, which is an app identity, not Mai’s user account. So the notebook may succeed under Mai’s `EXECUTE` access, while the agent fails because its own identity lacks `EXECUTE`.

So “The agent’s service principal has no `EXECUTE` on the function” is better because it names the identity that actually runs the call and the missing permission.

handoff_kept/check:0:1.text:
That idea gets one part right: a bigger model may remember and rewrite a bit better. But it misses the real bug. The loss happens at the hand-off, when the main agent only sees a helper’s final message and then restates it. More memory does not stop facts from being dropped.

The better first fix is: make helpers put every finding in their final message, and make the main agent pass that message on word for word. That protects the facts, like the order number, instead of trusting the model to remember them.

One question: if the helper found `order 4412`, what should you check in the final answer?

sort_changes/check:0:1.text:
`The eval set` is a reasonable concern because a small test set can give noisy results. A few questions can make a pattern look bigger or smaller than it really is. That part is true.

But it misses the main clue in this lesson. If the traces show the **same articles** went to the answer step, then retrieval is probably not the problem. The issue is later in the pipeline, where the model turns those articles into text.

So `The generation step, where the answer is written` is better because it matches the evidence from the traces. The articles stayed the same, but the answer changed, so you look at the prompt, the model, or the scorer.

provider_versions/check:2:0.text:
“Run `init` again every day” gets one thing right: it can make your laptop fetch a newer provider, so you may match what Spacelift sees that day.

But it misses the real problem. If your laptop and Spacelift run `init` at different times, they can still pick different provider versions. That means the plan can change again tomorrow. It is not a stable promise.

`Commit .terraform.lock.hcl` is better because it records the exact provider version once, so everyone uses the same one until someone intentionally updates it.

replay_tools/check:1:2.text:
“Make up a likely answer” gets one thing right: it tries to keep the run going. But it misses the main goal of a replay test. The point is not to be helpful. The point is to keep the world fixed so every agent design sees the same facts.

If you invent an answer, you hide a new tool call that was never in the recording. That can make two runs look the same when they are not.

Marking the call as `missing` is better because it tells you the agent left the frozen world. Then you can judge the run fairly and decide whether to record that call too.

wilson_interval/check:0:0.text:
“The leak rate is 0%” gets one part right: none of the `30` risky prompts slipped through in this sample. But it misses the main point. A sample of `30` is small, so `0` leaks does not prove the true leak rate is really zero. The Wilson interval says the true rate could still be as high as about `11%`.

So, “The leak rate is probably low, but could be as high as about `11%`” is better because it is honest about uncertainty. It uses the sample result, but it does not pretend the real rate must be exactly `0%`.

Would you like a quick intuition for why `0` out of `30` still allows room for risk?

failure_counts/check:2:2.text:
`“It uses more labels than you did”` gets one thing right: the model can only help if it is producing labels in the same set you use. But it misses the real check. More labels is not enough if the names mean different things. For example, your `repeated step` might be the model’s `looping`, and then the counts will be split or wrong.

What matters first is that its labels match yours on the 50 hand-labeled traces. That means the same failure gets the same label, so you can trust the counts and compare runs fairly.

apply_order/check:1:0.text:
`It creates A first, then B` gets one part right: Terraform does pick an order. But it misses the key point here. If `A` needs a value from `B`, and `B` needs a value from `A`, there is no valid first step. Neither one can be created before the other. That is a loop in the dependency graph, so Terraform cannot plan a safe order.

So `It stops with a Cycle error` is better because it says the real outcome: the resources wait on each other in a circle, and Terraform reports `Error: Cycle` instead of guessing an order.
